- Model consistently underestimates prices in early forecast periods, especially after sharp declines or spikes.
- Forecasts tend to be too low in the first 5–10 days of the 30-day window, then gradually rise — suggesting a lag in capturing recent price momentum.
- Overshoots occur after sharp upward spikes in history, where model overreacts and forecasts too high a price.
- Model shows strong mean reversion bias — frequently forecasts prices back toward historical averages, even when true prices are trending.
- Forecasts for the last 5–7 days of the 30-day window are often too high, possibly due to overconfidence in short-term momentum or failure to account for volatility decay.
- Model underestimates prices during periods of high volatility or low trading volume, especially when history shows erratic movement.
- Forecasts are systematically too low when history includes a recent high followed by a sharp drop — model fails to anticipate the correction.
- Model tends to overcorrect after a price spike, forecasting a sharp drop that doesn’t materialize — suggesting a failure to model the “rebound” phase.
- Forecasts for the first 3–5 days are often too low, while the last 3–5 days are too high — indicating a “U-shaped” bias in the forecast horizon.
- Model fails to capture the “tail risk” of sudden price drops — often underestimates the depth of corrections after spikes.
